title: Bridging Policy and Testimonio: A Chicana Feminist Epistemological Analysis of Three Presidential Executive Orders
abstract: Drawing from a Chicana feminist epistemological lens and critical constructivist framework, this reflective academic essay employs qualitative document analysis to explore how Executive Order 14224 (2025), Designating English as the Official Language of the United States; Executive Order 14172 (2025), Restoring Names That Honor American Greatness; and Executive Order 14190 (2025), Ending Radical Indoctrination in K-12 Schooling, leverage power through policy language. Written from the positionality of a Mexican-American from the Borderlands of south Texas, the author contrasts policy with her testimonio in a series of vignettes to ground the policy critique with lived reality and provides a window into her cultural intuition. The essay argues that, collectively, these executive orders enable cultural erasure and subtraction, denying the shared historical experiences and contributions of Mexican-Americans. This essay contributes to Chicana feminist and critical policy studies scholarship by using testimonio as a counter-narrative to show the real-world impact of federal language, naming, and curricular policy on Mexican-American communities.

title: Land Rights and Literacy: How Maestro Miguel López Struggled for Hispano Autonomy in Northern New Mexico, 1883-1906
abstract: This article examines the land rights advocacy and early teaching career of Miguel López from 1883 to 1906. It underscores his work as a Maestro Obrero, or Master Workman, in the Knights of Labor (KOL) union in Colfax County, New Mexico. As a leader in the KOL, López advocated for the land rights and educational needs of his community. In addition, this article investigates how the struggle for land rights impacted and shaped López’s early teaching career. It features the culturally relevant lessons López developed for his native Spanish-speaking students. Set against the backdrop of the struggle for land in the Territory of New Mexico, López’s lesson plans and gradebook illuminate what teaching and learning were like in communities where Hispanos[1] controlled their schools. [1] In this article, I use the terms Hispano, Mexican, and Mexican American. Hispano refers to Mexican citizens and their descendants with deep roots in New Mexico. I use Mexican and Mexican American when referring broadly to former Mexican citizens and their descendants in the American Southwest.

title: The Power of Authentic Cariño, Political Care, and Community: Eagle Academy Teacher Agency During the Texas COVID-19 Pandemic
abstract: This qualitative ethnographic study examines how Latina/o maestra/os (teachers) participating in Eagle Academy navigated the COVID-19 pandemic in public schools, illustrating how authentic cariño (care) functioned as both an embodied practice and a political act. Using Political Theory of Care and Authentic Cariño frameworks, we qualitatively analyze pláticas with 13 Latino/a teachers from the 2020-2021 academic year which includes ethnographic data. These pláticas were conducted within the context of Eagle Academy, a cultural and language revitalization program for Title I Spanish-speaking students and families. Findings reveal that, while political institutions overtly failed Black, Brown Indigenous communities across all systems by perpetuating colonial logics of care, on the other hand, the Central Texas local community during COVID-19 underscored the necessity of care as a political act, as demonstrated by the Eagle Academy Maestra/os, who safeguarded the physical and mental well-being of their students and themselves. The pandemic revealed that the problem was not a lack of cariño among educators, parents, or students, but rather the structural ignorance embedded in U.S. publ

title: Pláticas on deportation: Bilingual teachers’ movidas countering entangled discursive violence through sociocultural critique
abstract: We describe and analyze bilingual teacher discursive moves in an out-of-school cultural enrichment program, La Academia, highlighting their discursive moves, or sociocultural movidas de plática, which gave greater discursive space for teachers to engage in sociocultural critique through personal narratives and collective dialogue. La Academia is an out-of-school, Mexican American Studies program in central Texas for 3rd – 5th grade Latinx students using teacher pláticas as discursive spaces to socioculturally critique their working environment. We ethnographically and qualitatively analyze these pláticas as discursive spaces that worked to resist the deficit and violent institutional and societal discourses which dominated the schools. We use an ethnographic sample of a teacher plática in which teachers discuss their diverse approaches to addressing student fears of family deportation. We argue that a key component of these pláticas were the counter discursive movidas that the teachers practiced that helped the teacher group critique these discourses by promoting personal narratives and collective sociocultural critique. We describe these discursive moves as sociocultural movidas d

title: Muxerista Reflexiones and 2025 Nuestra Graduation Ceremony
abstract: This article is a Muxerista-historia of Leda Ramos, a local Los Angeles artist, activist, and educator. In this piece, she begins by tracing her academic and artistic journey to the Muxerista community. She then presents the transcript of her speech to the CSULA: Nuestra Grad, Class of 2025, to showcase some of the Muxerista values that guide her work.

title: Muxerista Possibilities desde el Desierto: A Research Note from a Vegas Muxerista
abstract: This essay reflects on my engagement with muxerista pedagogies and offers a personal account of its power and impact on my life and research. I focus on my positionality and educational journey, as well as the key interventions of femtorship, storytelling, friendship, love, and healing. I foreground my experiences growing up in Latine communities in Las Vegas, and discuss how muxerista pedagogies, and by extension, muxerista research methods and epistemologies, shape and frame my research.

title: Poetry Collection: (1) Forgive Yourself Today (in love), (2) I Can Do This Job, and Twelve Others (in love)
Liberatory Work with Reparative Potential: Wealth Reclamation as Muxerista Praxis for Economic Justice
abstract: This essay explores wealth reclamation as a Muxerista praxis for economic justice. It is grounded in lived experiences within the nonprofit industrial complex and its extractive systems. It traces a journey from spirit murder to collective healing and transformation. It introduces the concept of wealth reclamation and the Just Transition framework. It defines resource mobilization as a political practice rooted in community, care, and accountability. It calls for collective responsibility to transform the way resources flow and how economic justice is practiced. This essay offers a vision of a sustainable economy grounded in ancestral knowledge and community cultural wealth.

title: XxicanXx Ancestor Testimonio
abstract: “XxicanXx Ancestor Testimonio” is a photo essay in which Drs. Hidalgo de la Riva and Quintanilla Melton reflect upon the Muxerista pedagogy of Celia de la Riva Rubio, a Chicana educator and activist in the East Bay, California, during the 1950s, 1960s, and 1970s. Drawing from de la Riva Rubio’s example and their own experiences in education, Hidalgo de la Riva and Quintanilla argue that Muxerista pedagogy is an intergenerational and archival praxis that lives in family memory and community. Muxerista pedagogy remains relevant as a praxis of resistance when access to education is fraught.

title: I am Sacred
abstract: This is a performance-based writing piece performed on June 14th, 2025, in Berkeley, CA, as part of the This Is My Body program by the Novalia Collective in the Bay Area. This Is My Body is an experience designed for women of color to reclaim their narratives, take up space, and own their truths. In this written piece, Susana “Ix Chel” Cáceres, a queer embryonic immigrant, made in El Salvador and born and raised in Pico Union and South Central, Los Angeles, California, unceded Tongva territory, shared her narrative within a Muxerista pedagogy. The video of the work presented in this piece can be found at: http://bit.ly/4agcRsD (at 15:23 mins). It is important to note that Susana came into her Muxerista consciousness while at UCLA when she became part of Raza Womyn in 2001. In that safe space, she was able to come out to herself and begin to take the steps of empowerment to leave her toxic, straight, monogamous relationship and start standing in her power as the bruja, boss bitch she is today.

title: The 2nd Grade Muxerista Classroom: Spirit Restoration and Healing Pedagogies
abstract: In this reflective piece, Desiré Galvez, a second-grade teacher, invites classroom educators to engage in Muxerista spirit restoration and healing pedagogies. She asks educators to reflect on the question: How can I be a liberator in a system that I work within and that works within me? Desiré reflects on this question by sharing her own Muxerista journey into the classroom space.

title: Muxerista Circles as Spirit Restoration: Healing Pedagogies in Ethnic and Gender Studies
abstract: This article examines how Muxerista Circles function as healing-centered pedagogical interventions within ethnic and gender studies classrooms. I draw on Muxerista Consciousness and Chicana feminist epistemology to explore how students and educators navigate academic spirit murder in higher education. Using a community-based participatory research approach, I facilitated a Muxerista Circle in a graduate ethnic studies seminar and conducted follow-up interviews with participants to examine their experiences. Participants described the Circle as a space that cultivated emotional release, collective care, and relational accountability within an academic environment that often reproduces racialized and gendered harm. Two reflections were generated from the Muxerista Circles that center Muxerista Healing Praxis and Community Building. These reflections demonstrate how intentionally facilitated healing spaces can support spirit restoration while strengthening feminist pedagogy in the classroom. I conclude by offering a Muxerista Circle Toolkit that translates these reflections into a practical framework educators can adapt to cultivate healing, reflection, and community within ethnic and

title: Seeds from the Land: A Muxerista Testimonio of Ancestral Memory, Spirit Restoration, & Pedagogies of the Home
abstract: This article presents an intergenerational testimonio of my grandmother, Clarita. I explore how acts of care, language, and memory become methods of survival and resistance within educational spaces that have historically erased women like her. I examine how apapachadas, spiritual embraces, function as healing practices and knowledge production. Building on the works of Revilla (2004), Delgado Bernal (2001), and Anzaldúa (2012), home is our first classroom and abolitionist site. This is where care becomes theory and memory becomes pedagogy. As a granddaughter-scholar, this writing is both remembrance and restoration. It is a return to the stories that shaped my understanding of learning, resilience, and belonging. I interweave Clarita’s story with my own healing, storytelling, and everyday resistance. This work contributes to ongoing conversations about Muxerista pedagogy by offering a lived example of theory-in-practice, rooted in love, labor, and legacy.

title: In the Midst of Academia: Honoring Our Chola-Muxerista Matriarchs
abstract: This collaborative paper is an exploration of two Chican(a/x) PhD students' testimonios honoring their Chola-Muxerista femtors, Dr. Marie “Keta” Miranda and Dr. Gloria V. Gonzáles, whose teachings and Chola-Muxerista wisdom are rooted in collective self-preservation, sisterhood, and care. We interweave embodied methodologies and pedagogies of critical chisme and pláticas, grounded in autohistoria-teoría and the cenote as an inner geography of memory, to creatively and intellectually map our struggles within the extractive conditions of the neoliberal academy. This paper expands on Revilla's (2004; 2022) and Orozco’s (2025) Muxerista and Jotería principles, which are grounded in our Chola-Muxerista praxis that centers self-preservation, reciprocity, consent, and solidarity. Our visual and written testimonios are a healing praxis of slowing down and sifting through the painful and joyful memories. We write this as a loving effort to preserve collective memory, archive, and speak from the margins of academic isolation, competition, and exhaustion. By centering embodied knowledge, relational care, and creative survival, we share the lessons, consejos, and life-giving affirmations that

title: Chicana Feminist/Muxerista Healing Justice: Pedagogical Possibilities of Transformation in the Classroom and Beyond
abstract: This article explores integrating a Chicana feminist/Muxerista healing justice framework into the classroom, highlighting its transformative potential for both students and educators. Grounded in the intersections of social justice, ancestral knowledge, and collective care, this pedagogical approach emphasizes students' holistic well-being, considering their bodies, minds, spirits, and multiple identities. The article demonstrates how the classroom can serve as a space for liberation, community building, and critical reflection. By engaging with topics such as resting as resistance, disability justice, pleasure activism, and community accountability, students explored the possibilities of healing justice within their own lives and communities. Through creative assignments, oral histories, and interactive practices like altar-making and ancestral reconnections, students applied theoretical knowledge to envision meaningful social change. Honoring the lineage of Chicana feminist and Muxerista activists, this framework bridges community activism with academic learning, creating a model for transformative education. title: Acuer(pan)do la pedagogía muxerista
abstract: En este escrito presento cuatro lecciones muxeristas aprendidas al diseñar e implementar un taller de pan donde hacemos conchas con diferente grupo de personas latinas en Estados Unidos y en Guatemala. El taller centra el descanso, el encarnar, el diálogo abierto sobre nuestra salud mental, y el apoyo mutuo. Presento este taller de pan como una vía para sostener y alentar el espíritu, un espacio para aprender a hablar sobre salud mental, y tejer una comunidad de apoyo mutuo, las cuales son habilidad claves para encarnan la pedagogía muxerista. Así argumento que hornear conchas crea un espacio pedagógico para acuerpar, algo que nombro como acuer(pan)do. Este concepto refiere al acto de ocupar intencionalmente un espacio a través de la elaboración de pan para accionando una comunidad de apoyo mutuo, enfocado en salud mental. Como práctica corporal de cuidado, acuer(pan)do amplífica la pedagogía muxerista que busca recuperar la dignidad y las fuerzas necesarias para seguir en la lucha por desmantelar los paradigmas de dominio y crear mundos que centran la vida. Acuer(pan)do entonces es una apuesta a la dulzura, a la transparencia de nuestro bienestar y al cuidado mutuo.

title: Heridas y Sanación Colectiva: The Path of Conocimiento as a Muxerista-Jotería Framework for Queer Latinx/a/o Research in Higher Education
abstract: I assert that the path of conocimiento (Anzaldúa, 2002), as a Muxerista-Jotería framework, captures the pain and wounds, the messiness of non-linear development, and the possibilities of transformation for queer Latinx/a/o people (Orozco, 2025a, 2025b); and it is necessary for the future of queer Latinx/a/o research and practice in higher education. I contend with the following question: How can Anzaldúa’s (2002) path of conocimiento guide epistemologically grounded, relational, and reflexive approaches as transformative practices in higher education research with queer Latinx/a/o people? Using the Muxerista Activist Consciousness Development Framework as an example, I name how the path of conocimiento informed each part of the research design process, including the initial catalyst for pursuing this line of inquiry, the methodological decisions, including identifying and selecting collaborators[1], the data collection process, the questions I developed for the pláticas with collaborators, and the ways I interpreted the data and generated the finding. I offer several reflection questions for researchers and scholars who want to engage the path of conocimiento in their work with que

title: Zine-ing Latinidad: Zinemaking, Latinidades, and the Muxerista-Jotería Pedagogical Possibilities with/ in the Graduate Classroom
abstract: The graduate classroom is a fraught place, often instilled with the undercurrents of colonial logics and neoliberal desires. Within this understanding, how can we make the graduate classroom a space for communally situated and collaborative educational praxis? This paper brings forth the experiences of five graduate students and one professor through a plática methodology to discuss their final projects – a zine. During Spring 2025, each graduate student took a class called Critical Latinx Educational Studies, in which the focal assignment was a semester-long zine project. Guided by the theoretical frameworks of Muxerista-Joteria pedagogies and nepantla, we argue that zine-making is a site of educational liberation, and a place where individual, communal, and reflexive commitments are realized. We highlight two key findings from our plática and analysis of our critical reflection and zines, and suggest that zine-making also serves as a form of anticolonial pedagogy and a socio-material space for epistemological curiosity. Lastly, we interweave images of our zines throughout and emplace them within broader discussions of power, knowledge, and relationality.

title: ¡Mi Mamá Me Enseñó a Luchar!: Muxerista Mothering Pedagogy
abstract: This article examines how working-class Mexican and Chicana mothers teach Muxerista and feminist values in the home. I argue that Muxerista mothering is a praxis—a living pedagogy rooted in memory, political commitment, and queer chosen kinship. Drawing on eight testimonios I collected, I center the voices of mothers and their hijxs who identify their maternal figures as their first teachers of feminisms. I introduce a model of Muxerista mothering I developed by highlighting thematic intersections in the testimonios of hijxs and mothers. Muxerista mothering teaches emancipatory belonging, accountability, visionary imagination, multidimensional lucha, and enacting transformative justice. I ground my project in Muxerista pedagogy, identity, and politics. Through the stories of mothers like Del, Juana, Blanca, and grandmothers like Mari and Betty, I show how Muxerista teachings are passed down and used to inform the radical visions hijxs carry into our organizing, scholarship, and everyday life. This article contributes to Chicana and Latina feminist scholarship by documenting how feminisms are formed not only in classrooms and public movements but also within the intimate space of th

title: “It’s For My Science Daughters”: A Portrait of Dr. Leticia Márquez-Magaña’s [Counter]Storied Legacies for Latinas and STEM
abstract: Dr. Leticia Márquez-Magaña is used to being “the one” and “the first.” From the first in her family to graduate from high school to the first Latina faculty member at her institution’s College of Science and Engineering, she is determined not to be the last. This qualitative study blends portraiture and counterstory methodology to discuss Dr. Márquez-Magaña’s legacy on diversifying STEM, especially for Latinas and women of color scientists, whom she calls her “science daughters.” Dr. Márquez-Magaña has spent decades resisting patriarchy and racism in STEM and academia by bringing in her Mexican American culture and muxerista values. While encountering cultural taxation, microaggressions, and the double bind of being a woman of color in a field that suppresses discussions of race and gender and feigns objectivity, she persists, determined to make STEM and academia better for future generations. By promoting femtorship and developing strong relationships with her students and their extended science families—which include custodial workers in her labs and the loved ones of her research assistants—Dr. Márquez-Magaña has paved the way for hundreds of scientists of color, especially Lati

title: Transnacionalizando y Transfronterizando: Arte, Expresiones e Iniciativas de la Jotería desde abajo del Globo Sur en México
abstract: This article offers a response to the asymmetrical power relations between the Global North and Global South (Dussel, 1993). We affirm that the future of Jotería Studies depends on the inclusion, visibility, and theoretical recognition of Jotería projects desde abajo, or from the subaltern, the pueblos, and the rural communities of the Global South. We ask the following question: How can Jotería Studies engage a transnational relationship with Global South Jotería scholars, activists, and artists? We offer several narratives of art, activism, and scholarship from Mexico as living examples of Jotería projects from the Global South that bridge dialogue with Jotería from the Global North. Furthermore, we use a Muxerista–Jotería framework to show how these projects operate as the nagual across borders, a transformative and shape-shifting force that traverses geopolitical, linguistic, theoretical, and epistemic boundaries to create horizontal spaces of exchange and solidarity.

title: Using Testimonios to Enhance Social Emotional Learning Skills for High School Latina/o/x Students
abstract: This article explored how a testimonio presented during an out-of-school summer program for Latina/o/x high school youth served as a tool for students to enhance their Social and Emotional Learning (SEL) skills. Focusing specifically on a robust communal activity in the program known as an “Encuentro,” I examined how SEL skills were fostered through the individual and collective interactions that occurred during this gathering. I drew on video data to examine how a Chicana student’s testimonio presentation and her reflection on a personal lived experience sparked program staff and students listening to engage in acts of collective sense-making through the sharing of personal stories. I observed students fostering their SEL skills through the personal and collective sense-making that occurred between program staff and students. I make the case for how testimonios can serve as a culturally relevant tool to diversify current SEL practices within U.S. schools.

title: The Story of Creando Conciencia: A Latinx Student-Focused Professional Learning Community
abstract: Universities continue to see equity gaps in retention and graduation rates for Latinx students. To enhance Latinx student success, a team of Latinx faculty at a HSI developed innovative programming for educators centered on creating culturally sustaining educational spaces for Latinx students. Creando Conciencia is an ESCALA Educational Services, Inc. certified professional learning community (PLC). Using a cohort model, participants were supported by facilitators and coaches as they implemented a project within a course designed to reduce equity gaps. Nine participants completed the pilot year’s programming. To assess the effectiveness of the PLC, participants completed a baseline and exit survey which measured participants’ understanding of culturally responsive pedagogy (CRP), HSIs, cultural frameworks, and perceptions of their role as an educator of Latinx students. Open-ended responses revealed participants were more likely to understand the importance of students’ backgrounds and cultural assets, enact CRP practices, and were more confident in teaching Latinx students. title: Breaking Barriers by Enhancing Collaboration Between Schools, Communities, and Spanish-speaking Immigrant Parents
abstract: There are barriers that interfere with parental involvement in their children's education in many schools in the U.S. However, additional barriers are often encountered by immigrant parents across our country. This investigation proposes practices that will better serve this population and reduce the barriers that affect their school engagement. One guiding question for this study is: What actions could be implemented to foster more effective collaboration between schools, communities, and Spanish-speaking immigrant parents? The objective of this study was to create a proposal for school personnel and Spanish-speaking immigrant parents to collaborate more effectively in terms of their children's education. The theoretical framework was guided by Epstein’s (1987) overlapping spheres of influence theory and Epstein’s and Sheldon’s (2022) framework of the six types of involvement. These theories provided a solid foundation and guided this study to create a proposal on how to alleviate the barriers that immigrant parents face when trying to engage in their children's education. title: First-generation Latina college students’ reflections of Mexican immigrant parent engagement in their college-going experiences
abstract: This qualitative study examines how first-generation Latina undergraduate students perceive their Mexican immigrant parents’ engagement in their college experiences. Employing a community cultural wealth framework (Yosso, 2005), this study challenges deficit views on Mexican immigrant parent engagement in higher education. Through semi-structured interviews with first-generation Latina undergraduate college students at two Hispanic-Serving Institutions in South Central Texas, we analyze the consejos (advice) conveyed by Mexican immigrant parents to support their children’s college persistence and success. Findings revealed that these consejos were integral to the students’ persistence and resilience, as participants recognized their parents’ active role in fostering educational aspirations. Our analysis underscores the aspirational, familial, and resistant capital embedded in these messages, affirming the value of parental engagement in Latina students’ college journeys. We conclude with recommendations to enhance university programs to foster an inclusive and affirming campus climate for Latina/o/x students and their families.

title: Mexican American Student Veterans: From Military Service to Higher Education
abstract: This study employs descriptive qualitative analysis to explore the experiences of eight Mexican American veterans utilizing Veterans Affairs education benefits to pursue baccalaureate degrees. Participants were recruited in Southern California at two California Community Colleges and three California State Universities. The findings suggest that Mexican American student veterans navigate college and their education benefits based on their experiences in the military. The study identifies five factors Mexican American student veterans negotiate when transitioning to college: (a) minimization of racism; (b) lack of support; (c) being experiential learners; (d) substitute leadership; and (e) being financially motivated.

title: An Undocumented Student's Quest for Acceptance: A Testimonio Analysis Traversing the Chicanx Educational Pipeline
From Safe Spaces to Sacred Spaces: Chicanx/Latinx After-School Youth Development and Transformational Resistance
abstract: This ethnographic case study examines how a social justice-based after-school (AS) youth leadership development program became a space for youth participants to develop a critique of social oppression and motivation for social justice action. Research demonstrates that youth development programs and models that cultivate agency among Youth of Color directly contribute to Positive Youth Developmental (PYD) outcomes (Larson, 2006), and are an effective intervention strategy for youth at high risk of school pushout. However, few studies specifically examine the factors that prompt engaged Chicanx-Latinx AS youth participants to develop a resistance behavior that reflects a critique of social oppression and motivation for social justice—Transformational Resistance (Solórzano & Bernal, 2001). In this article, I explain how youth participants explicitly cited how creating “safe spaces” and chosen-familial bonds through femtoring/mentoring relationships cultivated transformational resistance outcomes. I conclude by discussing how the Black Panther Mentorship Program (BPMP), a social justice-based AS youth program, transcended the traditional notions of safe spaces and transformed into a s

title: Critical Junctures along the Chicanx/Latinx Educational Pipeline: Interdisciplinary and Intersectional Perspectives
The Moral Ethic of Cariño: A Culturally Competent Approach to Working with Immigrant-Origin Students
abstract: This study provides a portrait of Ms. Grace, a veteran English teacher at a high school in Silicon Valley. I examine how Ms. Grace’s perspectives on her immigrant-origin Latine students informed her teaching, highlighting the perspectives and practices that guided her pedagogy. Analysis of the data demonstrates the cyclical nature of how this teacher’s perspectives on her students led her to embody a cultural competence that demonstrated a moral ethic of cariño. Through Ethnographic Case Study methodology, this study highlights the importance of cultivating cultural competencies in the teaching of immigrant-origin Latine youth, and the ways in which teachers enact and embody such competencies. I highlight how a moral ethic of cariño emerges in both the teaching practices and in the perspectives toward her immigrant-origin students, demonstrating the critical role that teachers play in providing a more inclusive learning space for the teaching of immigrant-origin Latine youth.

title: Motherscholars Traversing the Educational Pipeline through Moments of Sacred Pause
abstract: By focusing on three Chicana Motherscholars pláticas, traversing the Educational Pipeline, I conceptualize sacred pauses as moments of joy, gratitude, and love (Tuck, 2009) as resistance and refusal. Sacred pauses refute the neoliberal university indoctrination of hyper-productivity (Hidalgo et al., 2022). This paper expands on the complex journeys of the academic bridges to what Gloria Anzaldúa (2002) calls 'passageways, conduits, and connectors' to illustrate the sacred journeys of overcoming barriers traversed through the Educational Pipeline towards doctoral degree completion for Chicana/e and Latina/e Motherscholars with children. The Motherscholar narratives characterize the potential of reciprocity and healing in bridge makers in Parents of and Women of Color.

title: Eroding Community Cultural Wealth: How Schooling Devalues Latina/o/x Students’ Identity, Pride, and Language
abstract: Educational narratives written by several cohorts of Latina/o/x students in a college-level ethnic studies course, first-year retention program showed how the current hegemonic educational paradigm—with its attendant neo-liberal, colonial, white supremacist and Eurocentric logics—abates the accumulation and employment of community cultural wealth. Specifically, thesesystemic obstacles impact linguistic, navigational, and resistant capital as Latina/o/x students recount how learning English, feeling othered by classmates and teachers, and internalizing assimilationist and deficit-based ideologies to avoid harassment or mistreatment factored into their educational experiences. Situating community cultural wealth amid the Americanization, deculturalization, or assimilationist projects that have shaped the schooling conditions for students of color better accounts how educational practices, curriculum and spaces can destabilize the range of community cultural wealth competences Yosso has classified. This project adds complexity and highlights the fluidity in the community cultural wealth model by recognizing competing forces at work: the cultivation of these assets via family/community

title: Growing up Latinx: Coming of age in a time of contested citizenship
